proposals.before: I would have Your Highness lift your eyes to Boyi's yielding and hold to the great worth Zizang's example: flee the jade carriage and refuse to mount it, cast off the realm as one casts off a shoe—perhaps to change shallow rivalry and restore the great wind of Wu.
proposals.after: I would have Your Highness lift your eyes to Mu Yi's superior benevolence and hold to the great worth of Zizang's example: flee the jade carriage and refuse to mount it, cast off the realm as one casts off a shoe—perhaps to change the custom of shallow rivalry and magnify the air of the state of Wu.
proposals.reason: Chinese 目夷 is Mu Yi, not Boyi (伯夷); 上仁之義 is superior benevolence, and 以大吳國之風 means to magnify Wu's ethos, not merely restore it.

proposals.before: My thought is that I would hear Your Highness lift your eyes to the yielding of Boyi above and hold to the great worth's conduct of Zizang; flee the jade carriage and not ride it, cast away the ten thousand chariots as one casts off shoes—perhaps to change the custom of shallow rivalry and enlarge the wind of great Wu.
proposals.after: My thought is that I would hear Your Highness lift your eyes to Mu Yi's righteousness of superior benevolence and hold to the great worth's conduct of Zizang; flee the jade carriage and not ride it, cast away the ten thousand chariots as one casts off shoes—perhaps to change the custom of shallow rivalry and enlarge the wind of the state of Wu.
proposals.reason: 目夷 is Mu Yi, not Boyi; 上仁 is 'superior benevolence,' not 'above' modifying Boyi.

proposals.before: In the first year of Tiancheng (560) he was promoted to palace attendant and national university libationer and went to Chang'an to welcome Emperor Xuan.
proposals.after: In the first year of Tianjia (560) he was promoted to palace attendant and national university libationer and went to Chang'an to welcome Emperor Xuan.
proposals.reason: Chinese 天嘉 is Tianjia, not Tiancheng; the year 560 matches Tianjia 1 of Chen.

proposals.before: In the first year of Tiancheng he was promoted to Palace Attendant and National University Libationer and went to Chang'an to welcome Emperor Xuan.
proposals.after: In the first year of Tianjia he was promoted to Palace Attendant and National University Libationer and went to Chang'an to welcome Emperor Xuan.
proposals.reason: Chinese 天嘉 is Tianjia, not Tiancheng.

proposals.before: Hongrang was plain and simple by nature, broadly learned and master of many subjects. In the first year of Tiancheng (560), though a commoner, he held the posts of minister of ceremonies and grand master of splendid happiness, with golden seal and purple ribbon.
proposals.after: Hongrang was plain and simple by nature, broadly learned and master of many subjects. In the first year of Tianjia (560), though a commoner, he held the posts of minister of ceremonies and grand master of splendid happiness, with golden seal and purple ribbon.
proposals.reason: Chinese 天嘉 is the Chen reign Tianjia, not Tiancheng; the parenthetical year 560 matches Tianjia 1.

proposals.before: Hongrang was plain and simple by nature, broadly learned and master of many subjects; in the first year of Tiancheng, as a commoner he held the post of Minister of Ceremonies and Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, with golden seal and purple ribbon.
proposals.after: Hongrang was plain and simple by nature, broadly learned and master of many subjects; in the first year of Tianjia, as a commoner he held the post of Minister of Ceremonies and Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, with golden seal and purple ribbon.
proposals.reason: Chinese 天嘉 is Tianjia; Tiancheng is a mistranslation of the reign name.

proposals.before: Under Tianchen he was in turn grand-academy doctor, chief steward to the prince of Luling, left assistant in the masters of writing, superintendent of the feathered forest guard, palace scatterer grandee, and director of the secretariat in charge of the national history.
proposals.after: Under Tianjia he was in turn grand-academy doctor, chief steward to the prince of Luling, left assistant in the masters of writing, superintendent of the feathered forest guard, palace scatterer grandee, and director of the secretariat in charge of the national history.
proposals.reason: Chinese 天嘉 is Tianjia; Tianchen is a corrupted rendering of the same reign name.

proposals.before: In the Tianchen era he successively served as grand-academy doctor, chief steward to the Prince of Luling, left assistant in the Masters of Writing, concurrently superintendent of the Feathered Forest guard, palace scatterer grandee, and director of the Secretariat, in charge of the national history.
proposals.after: In the Tianjia era he successively served as grand-academy doctor, chief steward to the Prince of Luling, left assistant in the Masters of Writing, concurrently superintendent of the Feathered Forest guard, palace scatterer grandee, and director of the Secretariat, in charge of the national history.
proposals.reason: Chinese 天嘉 is Tianjia; Tianchen does not match the source reign name.

proposals.before: He then went out to attend the mourning in person.
proposals.after: The Emperor then went out to attend the mourning in person.
proposals.reason: Chinese silent subject continues the imperial edict speaker (朕); literal 'He' obscures that the mourner is the emperor.

proposals.before: In Datong year eight the emperor finished his commentary on the Correct Sayings of Confucius and ordered the National University to expound the imperial interpretation.
proposals.after: In Datong year eight the emperor composed his commentary on the Correct Sayings of Confucius and ordered the National University to expound the imperial interpretation.
proposals.reason: Chinese 撰 means composed or wrote; the idiomatic 'finished' is not present in the source.

proposals.before: As a nobleman's son he was chosen to marry Princess Nan'a, daughter of Liang's Emperor Jianwen.
proposals.after: As a nobleman's son he was chosen to marry Princess Nansha, daughter of Liang's Emperor Jianwen.
proposals.reason: 南沙 is Nansha, not Nan'a; the English romanization misreads 沙.

proposals.before: As a nobleman's son he was chosen to marry the Princess of Nan'a—the daughter of Liang's Emperor Jianwen.
proposals.after: As a nobleman's son he was chosen to marry the Princess of Nansha—the daughter of Liang's Emperor Jianwen.
proposals.reason: 南沙 is Nansha, not Nan'a; the English romanization misreads 沙.

proposals.before: Once, after a banquet in the Fragrant-Accepting Pavilion, Emperor Gaozong kept Xian and commandant of the guards Fan Jun, moved to the mountain pavilion, and talked with them all day.
proposals.after: Once, after a banquet in the Fragrant-Accepting Pavilion, Emperor Gaozong kept Xian and the commandant of the guards Fan Jun, moved their seats to the mountain pavilion, and talked and feasted with them all day.
proposals.reason: Chinese 徙席山亭 and 談宴終日 require moving seats and feasting; idiomatic drops "seats," the article before the office, and the feast.

proposals.before: In year six he was named administrator of Wu but declined because his father was in office; he was made bright-martial general and inner administrator of Nankang instead.
proposals.after: In year six he was named administrator of Wu but firmly declined on account of his father's appointment privilege; he was made bright-martial general and inner administrator of Nankang instead.
proposals.reason: 以父任 means declining by reason of father's appointment/privilege (任), not clearly that the father was then currently in office.

proposals.before: His elder brother's son Jianyi had been left vice director; now Xian was right vice director. The secretariat called them the great and lesser vice directors, and the court took pride in the pair.
proposals.after: Earlier, Xian's eldest brother's son Jianyi had been left vice director; now Xian was right vice director. Within the secretariat they called Jianyi the great vice director and Xian the lesser vice director, and the court took pride in it.
proposals.reason: Chinese names 簡懿 as 大僕射 and 憲 as 小僕射 specifically; idiomatic collapses both labels.

proposals.before: When Prince Shixing Shulang rebelled, Xian directed the response and played a leading part in suppressing him.
proposals.after: When Prince Shixing Shuling rebelled, Xian directed the response and played a leading part in suppressing him.
proposals.reason: Chinese 叔陵 is Shuling, not Shulang.

proposals.before: When Prince Shixing Shulang committed his outrage, Xian directed deployments and took part with force.
proposals.after: When Prince Shixing Shuling committed his outrage, Xian directed deployments and took part with force.
proposals.reason: Chinese 叔陵 is Shuling, not Shulang.

proposals.before: In Zhide 1, the crown prince was capped, and in the second year he performed the libation ceremony. Xian then memorialized asking to resign, but the Later Lord refused, assigned him two attendants, advanced him to General of the Cloud Banner, and gave him a staff.
proposals.after: In Zhide 1, the crown prince was capped, and in the second year he performed the libation ceremony. Xian then memorialized asking to resign, but the Later Lord refused, assigned him two attendants, advanced him to General of the Cloud Banner, and established a staff for him.
proposals.reason: 置佐史 means establishing assistant officials/staff, not giving a walking staff; the literal already has the correct sense.

proposals.before: That summer, the crown prince was finally deposed as Prince of Wuxing.
proposals.after: That summer, the crown prince was finally deposed and made Prince of Wuxing.
proposals.reason: 廢太子為吳興王 means demoted the crown prince to Prince of Wuxing; English 'deposed as' wrongly reads as removal from that title.

proposals.before: In summer, the crown prince was finally deposed as Prince of Wuxing.
proposals.after: In summer, the crown prince was finally deposed and made Prince of Wuxing.
proposals.reason: 廢…為 marks appointment to the new title after deposition; 'deposed as' reverses the relation.

proposals.before: His eldest son Chengjia served the Sui as secretary aide and vice director of the National University.
proposals.after: His eldest son Chengjia served the Sui, rising to secretary aide and vice director of the National University.
proposals.reason: Chinese 仕隋至 marks attainment up to those offices; idiomatic “served … as” flattens 至.

proposals.before: The Southern Dynasties biography of Zhou She has the phrase "his nephew Hongzheng"; She was therefore Hongzheng's uncle.
proposals.after: The biography of Zhou She in the History of the Southern Dynasties has the phrase "his nephew Hongzheng"; She was therefore Hongzheng's paternal uncle.
proposals.reason: 南史 is the History of the Southern Dynasties, and 伯父 is specifically paternal uncle, not a generic uncle.

proposals.before: On "sent out as magistrate of Ye": Qian Daxin's Examination of the Twenty-Two Histories says the site of Liang's Ye county is unknown.
proposals.after: On "sent out as magistrate of Ye": Qian Daxin's Examination of Discrepancies in the Twenty-Two Histories says the site of Liang's Ye county is unknown.
proposals.reason: 廿二史考異 is Examination of Discrepancies in the Twenty-Two Histories; the idiomatic gloss omits "Discrepancies".

proposals.before: uncle the Attendant-in-Ordinary and Protector-General She raised them—changed according to the History of the Southern Dynasties.
proposals.after: paternal uncle the Attendant-in-Ordinary and Protector-General She raised them—changed according to the History of the Southern Dynasties.
proposals.reason: 伯父 is paternal uncle; the literal English omits that specificity while the Chinese collation restores 伯父.

decisions.after: I would have Your Highness uphold Mu Yi's principle of exalting benevolence and follow Zizang's example of great virtue: refuse the jade carriage, cast off the realm as one slips off a shoe, and thereby reform the custom of petty rivalry and magnify the spirit of the state of Wu.
decisions.reason: 目夷 is Mu Yi, not Boyi. 抗 governs his 上仁之義, while 以大吳國之風 means to magnify Wu's ethos. The proposal finds the real errors but remains awkward in English, so the full sentence is revised.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 抗目夷上仁之義，執子臧大賢之節……以大吳國之風

decisions.after: I hope to hear that Your Highness upholds Mu Yi's righteousness in exalting benevolence and adheres to Zizang's conduct as a great worthy; that you flee the jade carriage and do not mount it, and cast aside a realm of ten thousand chariots as though shedding a shoe—thus perhaps reforming the custom of shallow rivalry and magnifying the spirit of the state of Wu.
decisions.reason: The original misidentifies 目夷 as Boyi and misparses 上仁. The proposal fixes those errors but its English syntax remains strained, so the literal rendering is revised in full.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 抗目夷上仁之義，執子臧大賢之節

decisions.reason: 天嘉 is the Chen reign name Tianjia; Tiancheng is a different and unsupported reading. The supplied year AD 560 also agrees with Tianjia 1.
The literal field likewise misreads the explicit reign name 天嘉, which must be Tianjia.
天嘉初 means the beginning of the Tianjia era. Tiancheng is not the reign name in the Chinese.
The literal field has the same false Tiancheng reading for 天嘉; Tianjia is required.
天嘉中 means during the Tianjia era. Tianchen is a corrupted romanization not supported by the source.
The literal field also misrenders the explicit 天嘉 reign name as Tianchen; the proposed correction is exact.
The preceding edict speaks in the emperor's first person as 朕. The omitted subject of 便出臨哭 therefore remains the emperor, and naming him prevents a false pronoun reference to Hongzheng.
撰 means composed or wrote. The original claim that the emperor finished the commentary adds a completion sense absent from the Chinese.
南沙 is Nansha. Nan'a would require a different Chinese place-name, so the princess's title is genuinely misspelled in English.
The literal field has the same character-level error: 沙 is sha, making the title Princess of Nansha.

decisions.after: Once, after a banquet in the Fragrant-Accepting Pavilion, the other guests withdrew. Emperor Gaozong asked Xian and Commandant of the Guards Fan Jun to remain, moved with them to the mountain pavilion, and talked and feasted with them all day.
decisions.reason: The proposal correctly restores 席 and 宴, but 'kept Xian' is unnatural and it still omits 賓退之後. The revision renders the complete sequence and makes the three participants clear.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 賓退之後，高宗留憲與衛尉樊俊徙席山亭，談宴終日

decisions.after: In year six he was appointed Administrator of Wu, but firmly declined because his father had held the same post; he was made General of Illustrious Might and Inner Administrator of Nankang instead.
decisions.reason: 以父任 does not say that Xian's father was then in office or invoke a vague appointment privilege. Yuan Junzheng had previously served as Administrator of Wu, so Xian declined appointment to the same post.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 君正將之吳郡……除吳郡太守，以父任固辭不拜

decisions.after: Earlier, Xian's eldest brother Yuan Shu, posthumously known as Jianyi, had served as Left Vice Director; now Xian was Right Vice Director. Within the Secretariat, Yuan Shu was called the Senior Vice Director and Xian the Junior Vice Director, and the court considered this an honor.
decisions.reason: The proposal still invents a nephew by reading the source artifact 子 as part of 長兄簡懿子. The chapter names Yuan Shu as Xian's elder brother, Jianyi is Yuan Shu's posthumous name, and the parallel quotation in Taiping Yulan reads 簡懿為左僕射. The two offices belonged to the brothers.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 先是憲長兄簡懿為左僕射……臺省目簡懿為大僕射憲為小僕射

decisions.reason: 叔陵 is the personal name Shuling. Shulang does not match the Chinese and misnames the Prince of Shixing.
The literal field repeats the same name error: 叔陵 is Shuling, not Shulang.
佐史 are subordinate staff officers. 置佐史 therefore establishes an official staff for Xian; it cannot mean giving him a walking staff.
The construction 廢太子為吳興王 means that the crown prince was deposed and made Prince of Wuxing. 'Deposed as Prince of Wuxing' reverses the title change.
The literal field has the same syntactic reversal. 為 introduces the new title granted after deposition.
仕隋至 marks the highest offices Chengjia reached while serving Sui. 'Rising to' preserves 至 more accurately than merely saying he served as both.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 仕隋至祕書丞、國子司業

decisions.reason: 南史 is the History of the Southern Dynasties, and 伯父 specifically denotes a paternal uncle rather than an unspecified uncle.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 南史周捨傳……周弘正之伯父

decisions.reason: 考異 means an examination of discrepancies or textual differences. The original shortened the established title 廿二史考異 and lost its distinguishing word.

decisions.after: ‘Their paternal uncle, Attendant-in-Ordinary and Protector-General She, raised them’—emended according to the History of the Southern Dynasties.
decisions.reason: The collation note explicitly restores 伯父, which is paternal uncle. The proposal finds the real omission but leaves an ungrammatical lowercase fragment, so the complete note is revised.

claimRetractions.reason: The supposed son exists only because the source artifact 子 was mistaken for a kinship word. The parallel text reads 為, and Jianyi is the elder brother himself.
The invented uncle-nephew relationship depends entirely on the same 子/為 source artifact. Yuan Shu, posthumously Jianyi, was Yuan Xian's elder brother.

claimRevisions.reason: The English name claim must follow the corrected reading of 南沙 as Nansha.
The alternate English title claim repeats the same Nan'a misspelling and must read Nansha.
The structured noble title must use the same corrected Nansha romanization as the reviewed translation.
Jianyi is Yuan Shu's posthumous name, not the personal name of a supposed nephew.
